abstract: This report presents the Anthropic Economic Index analysis of AI adoption patterns across geographies and enterprise sectors as of September 2025. The research documents that Claude.ai usage has grown from 20% to 40% of US employees in two years—far faster than prior transformative technologies—but adoption remains highly concentrated geographically and by income level. Within the US, workforce composition and local economic factors matter more than income in determining adoption. Enterprise API usage shows 77% of business deployments use automation-dominant patterns for specialized tasks like coding, while consumer usage exhibits more balanced automation-augmentation patterns.
keyFindings: AI adoption in the US reached 40% of employees by 2025, up from 20% in 2023, representing unprecedented speed compared to electricity (30+ years), personal computers (20 years), and the internet (5 years)

Global Claude usage per capita is heavily concentrated in small, technologically advanced economies: Israel (7.0x expected usage), Singapore (4.57x), and Australia (4.10x), with strong positive correlation between GDP per capita and Claude adoption (0.7% usage increase per 1% income increase)

Within the US, DC leads per-capita adoption (3.82x population share), followed by Utah (3.78x), outpacing California (2.13x); income differences explain less than half the variation in cross-state adoption, suggesting local workforce composition matters significantly

Educational and scientific task usage grew from 15.3% to 19.6% of Claude.ai conversations over 8 months, while directive automation (complete task delegation) jumped from 27% to 39%, suggesting increased user trust and model reliability

Enterprise API usage differs from consumer use: 77% of business API deployments show automation patterns versus 50% for Claude.ai; API customers prefer higher-cost tasks despite price incentives, indicating capabilities and economic value drive adoption over cost considerations
methodology: This is a multi-part analysis combining three data sources: (1) longitudinal analysis of Claude.ai conversations across three periods (V1: December 2024-January 2025; V2: February-March 2025; V3: August 2025) to track usage pattern changes; (2) privacy-preserving geographic analysis of 1 million randomly sampled Claude.ai conversations from August 4-11, 2025, classified by IP geolocation to 150+ countries and US states; (3) analysis of first-party API customer transcripts using same privacy-preserving classification methods. Tasks were classified using O*NET occupational taxonomy and bottom-up user request clustering. Geographic analysis introduced the Anthropic AI Usage Index (AUI), calculated as country usage share divided by working-age population share. Automation vs. augmentation collaboration modes were tracked across time and geography. Statistical analysis included correlation analysis with GDP per capita, regression analysis controlling for task mix, and Lorenz curve concentration analysis.
qualifiers: Several limitations are noted: (1) Geographic analysis filtered cells with fewer than 15 conversations and 5 unique user accounts for privacy; (2) Utah's high usage ranking noted as possibly influenced by coordinated abuse activity, though robustness checks suggest this is not driving overall results; (3) IP geolocation excludes VPN, anycast, and hosting services, potentially underrepresenting some user types; (4) The comparison between V2 and V3 collaboration modes complicated by different Claude models used for classification (Sonnet 3.7 vs 4), though reanalysis confirmed directive trend; (5) Analysis uses conversations as unit of observation rather than unique users, so multiple conversations from same user may be included; (6) O*NET taxonomy designed for US labor market, creating potential misclassification for non-US contexts; (7) Context/complexity analysis based on output token length as proxy for task complexity, which does not capture all dimensions of complexity; (8) Causal interpretation of automation vs augmentation patterns limited—authors explicitly note uncertainty about whether growth reflects model capability improvements versus learning-by-doing versus user base changes; (9) API data represents early adopters and may not generalize to broader business adoption patterns.
